heading: Water selects the color palette
narration: Seawater filters wavelengths unevenly. Red light disappears quickly, while blue-green light travels farther.

heading: Water selects the color palette
narration: That makes blue-green emission efficient for signals, camouflage, and illumination in much of the ocean.

heading: Water selects the color palette
narration: Eyes evolve in the same optical environment, so many deep-sea animals are especially sensitive to those wavelengths.

heading: Water selects the color palette
narration: The result is a shared channel: light that can travel, and eyes prepared to receive it. But evolution exploits blind spots.

heading: Water selects the color palette

heading: One chemistry, many jobs
narration: Bioluminescence is light produced by a chemical reaction, often involving a light-emitting molecule called a luciferin and an enzyme or photoprotein.

heading: One chemistry, many jobs
narration: The exact chemistry varies among organisms. In blue-dominated seawater, blue-green light often travels efficiently, which helps explain the color of many marine signals.

heading: One chemistry, many jobs
narration: The same ability can serve opposing roles: an anglerfish lure attracts, counter-illumination hides, a flash can startle, and a glowing cloud can distract. A single animal may use more than one function.

args.title: THE SAME ABILITY, OPPOSING ROLES

heading: Why one flash can mean opposite things
narration: That is why the MBARI percentages need careful narration. They demonstrate how common light production was among animals observed in a large ROV dataset.

heading: The disclosure in the percentage
narration: When the percentage appears on screen, the label should read 'animals observed in MBARI's ROV dataset,' not 'all deep-sea animals.' That extra line is small, but it separates a real study result from an invented universal census.

args.caption: Animals observed in MBARI's ROV dataset, not all deep-sea animals

heading: The disclosure in the percentage
narration: The narration should also distinguish generated light from fluorescence before showing any glowing image.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: This episode should feel like a mechanism demonstration. Begin with darkness, add the chemical reaction as a clean original animation, then reuse the same burst of light in four contexts: lure, camouflage, warning, and communication.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: That structural repetition has meaning; the surrounding behavior changes the function. Do not use MBARI footage unless the individual asset has commercial rights clearance.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: MBARI reports that 76 percent of observed water-column creatures and 45 percent of observed bottom-dwelling creatures in its ROV work could produce light, from the surface to 4,000 meters.

args.caption: The surveyed range, from the surface to 4,000 metres

heading: Evidence limit
narration: Those percentages describe the surveyed animals researchers could see and classify. They are not a universal species census.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: Fluorescence is also different from bioluminescence: fluorescence re-emits incoming light, while bioluminescence generates light chemically.

heading: Closing
narration: The deep ocean is dark, but it is not visually silent. Life supplies its own signals.

heading: Closing
narration: The useful question is not only which animal glows, but what that light is doing at that exact moment.
